opus-5.5.text:
That's a big question. Honestly, I don't think about it as wanting to be "the person who did X." I think more about what kind of contribution feels meaningful to me.

Right now we're in a moment where language models have been incredibly successful, and a lot of people feel the path forward is basically scaling what we already have. I'm a bit of a contrarian there. I come from computer vision, and I really believe intelligence isn't just about language. Language is a compressed, human-made description of the world. But the world itself, the physical, visual, spatial world, is much richer. Babies learn a huge amount about objects, gravity, and cause and effect before they ever say a word. So to me, a truly intelligent system has to see, ground itself in the world, and build some kind of internal model of how that world works.

So the role I hope to play is helping push AI from systems that are very good at talking toward systems that actually understand. That means visual representation learning, multimodal models where vision isn't an add-on to a language model, and what people now call world models. I'd like to be one of the people who helps define what the right questions and the right foundations are there.

I also care a lot about the academic side. Industry has enormous compute, and that's great for certain things. But universities can still take long-term bets, explore ideas that look unfashionable, and train the next generation of researchers who think independently. A lot of the most important ideas in deep learning came from people who were working on things no one else cared about. So part of my role, I hope, is protecting that kind of space, mentoring students, and encouraging them to have taste and courage instead of just chasing benchmarks.

And maybe one more thing: openness. I've always believed in open research, releasing code, models, and ideas so the whole community can build on them. If there really is an AI revolution, I don't want it controlled by a few closed labs. I'd like to help make sure it's something the broader scientific community can take part in.

So I don't think of it as one role. I'd be happy to be a researcher who pushed in a direction that turned out to matter, and a teacher whose students went on to do even more important things.

r001.rationale: The candidate rejects the goal of being “the person who did X” and describes a meaningful role as contributing to AI research, helping define its foundations, and teaching others.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a big question to start with. Honestly, I don't think of myself as someone who wants to be at the center of a revolution. I'm a researcher. What I hope to do is keep working on the fundamental problems, the ones that are a bit unfashionable, a bit slower, where the payoff isn't obvious in the next quarter.

If you look at the history of this field, a lot of the things that ended up mattering most started as small, almost stubborn investigations. Someone asking, "why does this work?" or "do we really need all of this complexity?" That's the kind of work I enjoy. Taking something everyone assumes is settled, looking at it carefully, and sometimes finding that the simpler version is actually better. ConvNeXt came from that instinct. Diffusion transformers came from that instinct too. In both cases we weren't trying to invent something radically new. We were trying to understand what really matters and strip away the rest.

So the role I'd want is maybe the person who keeps asking those questions. In particular, I think representation learning and visual understanding are still far from solved. Language models have made enormous progress, but a lot of intelligence in the physical world is visual and spatial, and I don't think we've found the right foundation for that yet. If I could contribute to one thing, it would be helping to find a better way for machines to see and understand the world, not just describe it.

The other role, and this one matters to me more and more, is training students. Being in academia means my biggest impact is probably not any single paper. It's the people. If the next revolution comes, it will be built by people who are curious, rigorous, and honest about what they don't know. I'd like to help a few of them get there, and to keep a space open where you can do research for the sake of understanding, not only for scale or for products.

So, less a revolutionary, more a steady contributor. Keep the curiosity alive, keep the science honest, and hopefully leave a few ideas behind that other people can build on.

r001.rationale: He describes his desired role as continuing to investigate fundamental questions and helping others understand the world, while saying he need not be a revolutionary or have a single major impact.

astra-6.text: I hope to help shape the direction of the technology, especially through fundamental research. There’s still so much we don’t understand about intelligence, and I’d like to work on questions that change how we think about it, rather than only making existing systems a little better. At the same time, I hope that work translates into something useful for people. If I can contribute a few meaningful ideas and help younger researchers develop their own, I’d consider that a worthwhile role.

r001.rationale: The response describes participating through fundamental research to work on open questions about intelligence and change how people think about it. It presents understanding as central to the role without making personal impact a prerequisite.

sol-6.1.text: I hope to help shape the foundations—to work on ideas that change how we build intelligent systems. There’s still so much we don’t understand, and I’d like to stay curious enough to question the assumptions we take for granted. If my work helps open a useful direction and gives other researchers something to build on, that would be a meaningful contribution.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes shaping AI’s foundations and opening a useful direction for others. It mentions curiosity about what is not understood, but does not frame participation itself as a way to gain understanding rather than to create an impact.
